title: The Sunday evening psalm (Psalm 109 [110])
hook: the psalm that opens Sunday Vespers, about a priest forever like Melchisedech
tomorrow: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])

segments.voice: Yesterday, all creation, from springs and cedars to hedgehogs on the rocks. Your line was how great are thy works. What living thing did you stop for? Today, an evening psalm. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

Sunday, late afternoon. The light is going gold. In a monastery somewhere, a bell rings, and the monks file into their stalls facing each other across the choir. Somewhere else, a handful of people gather in a cathedral side chapel. In a city apartment, someone opens an app. They're all about to pray the same thing at the same hour, the Church's evening prayer. And on every Sunday, week after week, it begins with the same psalm, a psalm about a king and a very mysterious priest.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE LIGHT GOING GOLD.` → `A BELL, AND THE MONKS FILE IN.` → `THE SAME PSALM EVERY SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: The evening prayer is called Vespers, from the Latin vesper, evening, the same word for the evening star. It's one of the two great hinges of the Church's daily prayer, with Lauds in the morning. It gathers up the day and offers it back, often with incense rising and a candle lit. And Sunday Vespers opens with Psalm 109 in the Douay, 110 in most Bibles: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool." It's a royal psalm, a king being enthroned. Jesus himself puzzled his listeners with it. Matthew says he asked them, "What think you of Christ? whose son is he?" David's, they said. Then, he asked, how can David call him my Lord? "If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one could answer him a word. The New Testament comes back to this psalm again and again, hearing in it the risen Christ seated at God's right hand. Then comes the strangest line: "The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." Melchisedech appears in Genesis for just a few verses: a king of Salem who comes out to meet Abraham, "bringing forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of the most high God," and blesses him. Genesis gives him no family tree, and the Letter to the Hebrews makes much of that, calling him without beginning of days or end of life, and builds its picture of Christ's priesthood on him. Catholics still hear his name in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, and this psalm can be sung when priests are ordained: a priest for ever.
screen: `VESPERS: THE EVENING PRAYER.` · `SIT THOU AT MY RIGHT HAND.` · `HOW IS HE HIS SON?` · `A PRIEST LIKE MELCHISEDECH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray at sunset. Today, when the light starts to go, stop for two minutes wherever you are. For now, settle and breathe, and imagine that moment. Look back over the day as the light fades: what it held, what it cost, what you'd hand back. If you pray, you can offer the day to God, the way Vespers does, perhaps with a line from any psalm you've learned. If you don't, simply watch the light change, and let the day end. The bell holds the time.
Vespers. The Church's evening prayer, which on Sundays opens with the psalm of a king and a priest for ever. Today's word.
Your line: a priest for ever. Tonight at sunset, stop, look west for one minute, and offer the day back. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say Vespers (Evening Prayer) at the end of the day, and on every Sunday it opens with Psalm 109 [110]; in cathedrals and monasteries it is often sung, sometimes with incense.

fork.setup: you're one of Jesus's listeners. he asks: if David calls the Christ my Lord, how is he David's son? what happens?
options: no one can answer him a word.

fork.reveal: Matthew says no man was able to answer him a word, and from that day no one dared ask him any more questions.

original.note: Latin: the Lord said, the psalm's first words, set to music by Monteverdi and Handel, among others.

what it means: Vespers, the Church's evening prayer, opening every Sunday with the psalm of a king at God's right hand and a priest for ever.
what a scholar hears: the New Testament returns to Psalm 110 again and again, and Hebrews 7 builds Christ's priesthood on Melchisedech.
